meta.scope: Characteristic Paris public-realm signatures: exceptional transit entrances, drinking-water objects, public clocks, sanitary heritage, civic datum stones and individually storied street furniture
meta.method: A second-wave Paris lane screened serial public objects broadly but retained only named or individually defensible walking objectives. Every retained row has an exact feature or access pin, current public visibility or published access, at least two useful sources including an operator, municipal, public-institution or heritage-register source, a score of at least 19 with story and walkability at least 4, all-high confidence and a global 120 m catalogue review.
meta.serial_object_rule: Membership in a Paris-wide series is not sufficient. A retained series member must have a unique surviving type, documented relocation, first-of-kind status, exceptional restoration or a location-specific story that makes the individual object the objective.
meta.note: The parent run completed cross-lane review and imported the 12 retained rows as draft-quality candidates. Do not reimport; field-test and editorial promotion remain pending.

category_contract.label: Street furniture
category_contract.definition: Individually distinctive, designed objects installed to make public space work: transit entrances, public water points, public clocks, kiosks, sanitary structures, civic measurement or boundary markers, lighting and comparable small-scale civic infrastructure.
include_when: The object is a discrete walking objective with an exact feature or access pin.
It has an individual design, survival, first-of-kind, relocation, restoration or civic-use story rather than only membership in a serial inventory.
It is currently visible from public space or has current, practical public access stated by its operator.
Its main identity is a designed civic utility or public-realm fitting rather than a building, museum collection or free-standing commemorative monument.
exclude_when: Generic benches, ordinary lamp posts, current news kiosks, standard sanisettes, normal Metro surrounds and modern Morris columns without an individual story.
A decorative fountain whose primary identity is monumental sculpture; use monument or streetart instead.
A marker whose only value is a generic serial survey or commemorative plaque; use plaque or history unless the object function itself is the story.
Objects inside private courtyards, behind unconfirmed gates or with only a venue-centroid coordinate.

Vienna Stadtbahn entrances and historic public clocks
Lisbon quiosques and distinctive drinking fountains

included.n: Fontaine à l'Albien de la place Paul-Verlaine
included.s: One of Paris's three artesian fountains lifts mineral-rich water from an aquifer more than 600 metres below the Butte-aux-Cailles.
included.q: Fontaine Albien place Paul Verlaine Butte aux Cailles Paris
included.w: Taste only if the live status still says available. The unusual encounter is geological and mechanical: deep warm water is pumped, stripped of excess iron and cooled before it reaches this small neighbourhood tap.

facts.claim: Eau de Paris describes this as one of the capital's three artesian fountains, drawing Albien water from more than 600 metres underground.
The current fountain was inaugurated in 1999; its water is pumped, de-ironed and cooled before distribution.
Eau de Paris reported the fountain back in service on 29 January 2026, and the official drinking-fountain record 450071492 is currently marked available.

included.n: Horloge de Charles V du Palais de la Cité
included.a: Tour de l'Horloge, 2 boulevard du Palais
included.s: Paris's first public clock still faces the street from the medieval palace tower where Charles V commissioned it in 1370.
included.q: Horloge Charles V Tour de l Horloge boulevard du Palais Paris
included.w: Stand across boulevard du Palais and read the dial as civic infrastructure rather than façade ornament. For the first time, Parisians could take the city's time from a public clock instead of a private or church signal.

facts.claim: Paris Musées identifies the tower clock as the first public clock in Paris.

Ville de Paris says Charles V commissioned the clock in 1370, that it entered service in 1371, and that the dial was restored in 2012 using archival material from the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
A named feature record fixes the pin on the exterior dial rather than at the Conciergerie or courthouse centroid.

included.n: Borne milliaire du 85 rue de Vaugirard
included.a: 85 rue de Vaugirard, angle rue Littré
included.s: Paris's last royal road milestone marks one thousand toises from Notre-Dame with a single cut in its granite crown.
included.q: dernière borne milliaire 85 rue de Vaugirard Paris
included.w: Look for a granite block partly swallowed by the school wall. The vertical notch is the route number one: one thousand toises from the old measuring origin at Notre-Dame; the smoothed oval below likely once held a royal lily.
aliases: Borne des mille toises rue de Vaugirard

facts.claim: The Société historique du 6e identifies the granite object as Paris's last surviving royal road milestone and locates it at 85 rue de Vaugirard at rue Littré.
Its single vertical notch denotes the first thousand-toise interval measured from the centre of Notre-Dame's façade; the smooth oval probably held a fleur-de-lys erased during the Revolution.
Object-focused photography documents the milestone embedded at the public-street edge of 85 rue de Vaugirard and supplies the feature coordinate.

included.n: Borne-limite de Louis XV de la rue de Charenton
included.s: Half original and half reconstruction, a 1726–27 royal building-limit plaque survives where Paris once stopped and fields began.
included.q: borne limite Louis XV 304 rue de Charenton Paris
included.w: Look up between the windows and find the seam between survival and reconstruction. One half was rediscovered in 1910 serving as a back-shop floor tile; the completed inscription returned to the street as evidence of an earlier Paris edge.
aliases: Plaque des anciennes limites de Paris rue de Charenton

external_ids.commons_file: Plaque Anciennes Limites Paris Rue Charenton - Paris XII (FR75) - 2024-08-28 - 1.jpg

facts.claim: A detailed heritage account identifies the façade plaque as one of two surviving examples from 294 Louis-XV building-limit markers and records its public address at 304 rue de Charenton.
The plaque was installed at the old urban edge on 29 December 1727; Lucien Lambeau found half of it in a back-shop floor in 1910, after which the missing part was reconstructed.
Object-specific photography dated 28 August 2024 documents the plaque on the same publicly visible façade and supplies the practical pin.

included.s: A tiny 1806 street fountain translates an Egyptian temple façade into Napoleonic water infrastructure.
included.q: Fontaine du Fellah 42 rue de Sèvres Paris
included.w: Read the niche from pediment to basin. The so-called fellah may draw on an ancient statue of Antinous, while the whole miniature temple belongs to Napoleon's campaign to bring free water into the street.

facts.claim: Ville de Paris dates the neo-Egyptian fountain to 1806 and attributes it to engineer François-Jean Bralle and sculptor Pierre-Nicolas Beauvallet.
Paris Musées identifies the address as 42 rue de Sèvres and explains that the figure called a fellah more closely evokes Antinous, favourite of Hadrian.
The municipal 2024 walking article illustrates the fountain in place, while named mapped object node 4376593595 supplies the exact façade pin.

included.a: 129 rue Saint-Martin, angle rue de Venise
included.s: A compact 1733 utility fountain carries the name of a medieval water source and survives relocation around the remaking of Beaubourg.
included.q: Fontaine Maubuée 129 rue Saint Martin rue de Venise Paris
included.w: Notice how little street space it claims: early public fountains were practical taps before they became urban spectacles. Then compare its present corner with the old records—the entire stone face moved here when Beaubourg was remade.
aliases: Fontaine de la rue de Venise

facts.claim: The Ministry of Culture register identifies Fontaine Maubuée as protected historic architecture; its register location field is historical and is not used for the present pin.
Ville de Paris presents the 1733 Maubuée as an example of the small, lightly decorated utility fountains that supplied neighbourhood water.

Paris Musées records that the fountain was once fed by the Belleville aqueduct and was relocated from its former Simon-le-Franc corner to 129 rue Saint-Martin at rue de Venise during the Beaubourg area's redevelopment.
Eau de Paris identifies the object visible today as the 1733 fountain by Jean and Jean-Baptiste Augustin Beausire and states that water no longer flows from it.
Object-specific September 2024 and 2025 images document the fountain at its present public façade location; named mapped node 7616246086 supplies the object pin.

category_coverage_audit.serial_discipline: No ordinary Guimard surround, conventional Wallace caryatid or Morris column was retained merely because the type is characteristic of Paris.
category_coverage_audit.global_category_recommendation: Use the already registered globally reusable streetfurniture category. No Paris-only subcategory is warranted; subtype metadata can carry entrance, water, clock, sanitation and datum distinctions.

pin_audit.review_result: All 12 retained pins were independently rechecked. Nine use an official feature point, named object/access node or named object-footprint centroid; Trocadéro uses the operator-specified exit-1 access node; two embedded façade markers use bounded frontage/photo pins. Corrections replaced photo or generic coordinates for the Kiosque, the Wallace applique, Charles V's clock, the Arago vespasienne, the Fellah and Maubuée. Porte Dauphine was disambiguated from the separate simple Foch/Bugeaud surround and fixed to covered-model node 5313588566.
facade_level_caveats: Borne milliaire rue de Vaugirard: cadastre-sourced 85 frontage point checked against the embedded-wall image and rue Littré cue, within about 5 m.
Borne-limite rue de Charenton: current object-focused façade photograph, approach within about 10 m; use the 304–306 frontage cue.

proximity_audit.catalogue_scope: all 17,328 catalogue rows, with normalized Paris names and aliases, available stable identifiers and haversine review at 120 m
proximity_audit.dense_city_rule: Under 30 m is presumed duplicate; 30–119 m requires an explicit named distinct-place review. Distances are rounded in row summaries; raw checks were used for the threshold.
named_dense_reviews: Wallace applique versus Fontaine Cuvier (31.6 m) and Jardin des Plantes cedar (106.9 m): potable wall utility versus monumental fountain and living tree.
Trocadéro lavatories versus Carette (112 m): working sanitary interior versus café.
Fontaine du Fellah versus Chapelle Saint-Vincent-de-Paul (56.8 m after object-pin correction): exterior Napoleonic water object versus religious interior.
proximity_audit.internal_candidate_rule: Every retained pair from 30–119 m would require a named review; none exists. The closest retained pair is the Vaugirard milestone and Fontaine du Fellah at 357.2 m.

access_caveats: Jardin de Reuilly has municipal opening hours and can close for weather; fountain availability is also subject to maintenance or winterisation.
Trocadéro lavatories are a paid working amenity with the operator's published daily hours; recheck service notices before relying on access.
Historic exterior fountains and the boulevard Arago vespasienne are retained for viewing; this dossier does not promise that they flow, are potable or remain usable.
The drinking-water dataset is a dated snapshot. Same-day Eau de Paris maintenance status supersedes the dossier if drinking is the aim.
The Palais-Royal cannon, southern meridian marker and other proposed retags retain their existing park or garden access caveats; retagging does not erase them.
source_consistency_audit: Official accounts disagree on the year Fontaine Maubuée was dismantled or moved (Eau de Paris gives 1937; Paris Musées gives a 1970 move during Beaubourg redevelopment). The retained copy asserts only the well-supported relocation and present corner, not a year.
The Vaugirard milestone's erased fleur-de-lys and the Fellah figure's Antinous identification remain explicitly probable or conditional, matching their sources.

The Trocadéro page evokes the Paris of the 1920s but dates preserved stylistic elements tentatively to 1900–1910; retained copy calls the facility historic Art Nouveau and makes no unsupported construction-year claim.
